title: Low distant earthquake counts were more common after than before M7.5+ centers under yearly shifts in ComCat, 2001-2024
abstract: We tested whether low distant earthquake counts were more common after than before 125 M7.5+ centers in a fixed ComCat snapshot. Neighbors had M at least 5.5 and distance above 500 km. Each five-day count was low if it was below the exact tenth percentile for control times in the same year. There were 15 low after windows and 7 low before windows, a difference of 6.4 percentage points. In 19,999 trials with shared yearly time shifts, the one-sided p-value was 0.03415. The central 95% shift range was -6.4 to 6.4 points. This is a reference range, not an effect confidence interval. The later 2013-2024 subset gave a smaller 3.45-point difference and p=0.27525. A delayed-window check retained a positive contrast. This follow-up uses the same source as prior campaign work and is not independent confirmation. Selection, mixed magnitudes, missed detections and the time-shift assumption prevent a causal claim about earthquake suppression. Code, aggregate evidence, source hashes, an independent numerical audit and a chart are included.

display.caption: The observed paired low-count contrast and the shared-shift reference. Ranges are null reference ranges, not confidence intervals. Secondary settings use the same catalog.
